title: Recipeview: validate a nested edit before replacing children
focus: parent-child CRUD, partial edits and SQLite transactions
before: Nested recipe payloads could contain malformed ingredient/step values, blank edits were silently ignored, and IDs/dates were accepted by loose conversions.
after: A shared request boundary rejects malformed nested values and noncanonical IDs before handlers mutate rows. Recipe edits retain omitted children; valid replacements and search reindexing remain transactional. The app can be imported without binding a development port.
model: Dishes own recipes. Recipes own ordered ingredients, steps and cook logs; logs can own photos. Tags and the search_index support discovery. SQLite stores relationships; photo files live separately under RECIPE_LAB_DATA/photos.
concept:
A recipe editor often submits a complete ingredient list, so replacing children can be easier to understand than diffing each row. That design is safe only when validation and transaction boundaries are clear. Omitting ingredients means preserve them; sending [] means intentionally remove all. Reject a malformed row before deleting the old children, so a typo does not erase an otherwise valid recipe.

Search is another representation of the same domain data. Renaming a recipe updates its searchable context through reindexRecipeTree. The SQL transaction includes the parent edit, child replacement and search-index writes. Photo files cannot participate in a SQLite transaction, so deletion collects filenames before the database cascade and removes files after commit. A file-removal failure requires separate cleanup policy.

A quantity is a number or a deliberate blank, not an arbitrary object coerced to zero. The browser parses kitchen fractions before sending JSON. The API validates nonnegative ingredient quantities and positive recipe yield. Canonical positive integer IDs reject strings such as 1e2 rather than interpreting them as another record. This remains a local personal recipe app without multi-user authorization.
example: Create Pasta with a Weeknight recipe, one ingredient and one step. PATCH only title: both child lists remain. Send title Changed with a negative ingredient quantity: return 400 and preserve parent, children and search data. Deleting the dish cascades its recipes and removes their search entries.
exercises: Show ingredient-row validation beside the offending row.
Add a preview of scaled ingredient quantities without saving the scale.
Force a search-index write failure and verify the recipe edit rolls back.
Design stable child IDs if ingredients gain independent history.
answers: Keep the entered string and display its parse error; do not drop the row silently. Match the API domain rule after fraction parsing.
Compute quantity times desiredYield/originalYield as derived state. Keep the saved recipe unchanged until a separate edit is confirmed.
Use a fresh SQLite fixture and trigger failure after the parent update; assert the title and children retain their prior values.
Replace wholesale deletion with explicit create/update/delete operations keyed by ingredient ID. Explain ordering independently from identity and add conflict handling for concurrent editors.

title: Calendar + Jobtrack: validate the whole backup
focus: runtime schemas, nested records and import boundaries
before: Backup parsing checked only outer arrays/settings presence, so malformed events, recurrence, application history or duplicate IDs could reach the stores.
after: Backup parsing validates supported version, settings, category/event/application IDs, real dates, recurrence bounds, nested history and salary relationships before approving replacement.
model: The browser stores calendar events, categories, job applications and settings with Zustand/localStorage. Events can recur and reference job IDs. Applications have a current stage plus StageChange history. A Backup contains all four stores, app marker, version and exportedAt.
concept:
Casting JSON to Backup tells TypeScript to trust the programmer; it does not inspect the file. A valid outer object can still contain events:[null] or recurrence.interval=0. The latter can break recurrence generation or create excessive work. Validate nested values at the import boundary before passing them to any replaceAll action.

Duplicate IDs are a data-integrity problem even when every individual row is otherwise valid. React keys, store updates and references all rely on identity. The validator checks uniqueness within each record collection and each application history. It validates real calendar dates and increasing local event times without converting local appointments into UTC instants. An unknown category ID remains compatible with the existing display fallback.

The parser is pure: it returns either a validated backup or an error. Purity makes malformed cases easy to test without touching storage. Actual replacement still spans multiple localStorage-backed stores; validating first prevents malformed input from causing partial replacement, but a quota failure during later writes is a separate atomicity problem. A future redesign could store one versioned document or use one IndexedDB transaction.
example: A backup created by buildBackup still imports. Change an event start to 2026-02-30T09:00, set recurrence interval to zero, duplicate an ID, empty required application history or invert salary bounds: parseBackup returns an error before store replacement.
exercises: Display an import summary before replacing local data.
Show a helpful field path in validation errors.
Simulate storage failure between replacing two stores.
Move backup replacement to a single transactional persistence boundary.
answers: Count validated events/applications/categories and show exportedAt. Do not mutate stores until the user chooses the replacement action.
Carry the collection index and field name through validation, such as events[2].recurrence.interval, while keeping raw file contents out of generic error logs.
Use disposable storage and throw on the second write. Observe which stores changed and document the gap rather than asserting an unsupported all-or-nothing guarantee.
Use a single IndexedDB transaction or one versioned localStorage value. Plan migration and publish UI state only after the commit succeeds.

title: DevDeck: safe progress restore
focus: validating persisted state and atomic IndexedDB replacement
before: Import validation checked only a few outer fields; malformed scheduler values/settings or duplicate card IDs could enter a restore. Unknown-card logs were retained. One existing learning snippet exceeded its tested mobile length limit.
after: A complete import validator runs before the replacement transaction. It checks state/log/settings/meta values and unique card IDs; unknown-card states and logs are omitted consistently, missing known states are recreated, and rejected imports preserve progress. The long worked snippet was shortened without changing its behavior.
model: Bundled cards and decks provide learning content. ReviewState tracks cardId, ease, intervalDays, due, status, learningStepIndex, lapses and reps. ReviewLog records a grade/time. Settings and Meta hold study limits and streaks. Dexie wraps IndexedDB transactions.
concept:
A backup is not trusted merely because it has the right version. A negative due time, impossible grade or duplicate card state can corrupt scheduling even if IndexedDB accepts the value. validateImport checks the full structure before importData opens its write transaction. The transaction then clears old progress and inserts the validated replacement, so an insertion failure rolls back the clear.

Content evolves independently of progress. The chosen policy ignores states and logs for card IDs no longer bundled, and creates new states for known cards absent from the backup. This preserves useful progress while avoiding orphan logs. The returned count means known states restored, not total cards after missing-state recreation.

The test uses fake-indexeddb to exercise the actual Dexie methods and compares stored state/settings/meta after rejected imports. Chromium is a separate check of actual browser startup and interaction. The existing content QA tests also protect the learning experience: a 15-line nested-conditional example was shortened to fit the existing 12-line rule while retaining the same four input outcomes. This app is a browser persistence study case; it does not contain a server CRUD API.
example: Export fresh progress, set one card reps to 7 and restore only that state: the card keeps 7 reps and missing cards receive new states. Include one unknown-card log: it is omitted. A negative due value, duplicate state ID, invalid study limit or impossible metadata date rejects before any stored progress changes.
exercises: Preview how many states will be restored, ignored and recreated.
Explain one scheduler field with an before/after grade example.
Force an IndexedDB insert failure after clear and verify rollback.
Add editable learner-created cards with stable identity.
answers: Validate first, compare IDs with the bundled content and show all three counts without writing.
Pick an existing schedule test and trace due/status/intervalDays for Again versus Good using a fixed clock.
Use a transaction hook or invalid storage operation in an isolated database and compare all affected tables with the original export.
Separate bundled content from learner-owned content, avoid overwriting custom cards in seedAndLoad and define how exports include card definitions and progress references.

title: Organized Desktop Job Track: precise optional edits
focus: null versus omission, calendar validation and repeat-safe commands
before: Blank optional fields transformed to undefined and could not be cleared by partial updates; blank salary coerced to zero. Date shape checks accepted impossible dates and repeated same-status transitions returned an error.
after: Blank optional edits explicitly clear nullable fields, omitted fields remain unchanged, blank salaries remain null, and real dates are validated. IDs and sorting are deterministic; a repeated same-status transition returns the existing record without touching its timestamp.
model: Users authenticate with a JWT and own applications in SQLite. Each application stores company, role, location, URL, salary range, applied/next-step dates, status and notes. ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS defines valid workflow moves. The selected project is the root client/server app, not the other nested projects in this folder.
concept:
Partial update has three meanings: omitted means keep the old value, null means clear it, and a concrete value means replace it. An empty HTML text input is a string, so the boundary must map it deliberately. Converting blank to undefined removes the caller's intent to clear; Number("") creates zero, which incorrectly claims a known salary.

Cross-field validation belongs after merging a partial update with stored data. A request containing only salary_max=50 can violate the saved salary_min=100 even if the request schema sees only one field. The existing merged salary guard is retained and tested. Real YYYY-MM-DD validation compares the parsed label, so February 30 cannot silently roll into March.

A status command sets a desired state. Repeating the current state now returns that same record without updating updated_at. Other transitions still use ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS. This is a narrow retry guarantee; POST creation still needs a separate idempotency design. JWT ownership checks remain on every application path. JOB_TRACK_DATA_DIR lets tests use a fresh temporary database instead of touching the development data directory.
example: Create an application with blank salary fields: both are null. PUT notes and next_step_date as empty strings: both clear while company remains. After setting salary 100–200, a partial max=50 edit returns 400. Repeating the current status leaves updated_at unchanged; another signed-in user cannot edit the record.
exercises: Show unknown salary distinctly from zero salary.
Add an explicit Clear next-step date button.
Test simultaneous sorting ties across pages.
Add an application stage-history table transactionally.
answers: Render null as Not provided and zero as a known number if the domain permits it; avoid truthiness tests that merge these cases.
Send an explicit blank/null contract supported by the API rather than omitting the field, then verify the next read returns null.
Seed equal sort values and assert stable ID tie-breaking across repeated page reads; document pagination behavior when data changes.
Write the status change and history event in one SQLite transaction, preserve no-op behavior and test a late history failure leaves the original status unchanged.
